To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
some peptides interact with P- glycoprotein and inhibit the transport of chemotherapeutic drugs, and this inhibition is correlated with peptide binding to P-glycoproten.
linear and cyclic hydrophilic peptides can be used as substrates and as modulators of P- glycoprotein.
hydrophobic linear and cyclic peptides are substrates and modulator for P-glycoproteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of peptide substrates and modulator of P-glyco protein.
the identification and characterization of peptide substrates and modulating agents of P-glyco protein, a multidrug transporter that confers multidrug resistance ( MDR ) on tumor cells.
the interaction of linear and cyclic hydrophilic and hydrophobic peptides with P-gp, the multidrug transporter, and the effect of this interaction on drug accumulation and toxicity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the interaction of peptides with the P-glyco protein is not a simple phenomenon, but is dependent on the structure and the physicochemical properties of the peptide, as well as on the experimental conditions used.
peptides that interact with P-gp in the fluorescence-quenching assays are also capable of inhibiting drug transport and of restoring drug accumulation to the levels found in sensitive cells.
peptides can interact with P-gp in a manner that is dependent on their hydrophobicity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the peptides that bind to P-glycoproten, and thus block drug efflux, are those that are hydrophobic, and thus are able to cross the plasma membrane.
hydrophobic peptides can be divided into two classes: those that bind P-glycoproteins and those that do not.

peptides that interact with the drug-binding site of P-glyco protein can be identified by a fluorescence-quenchin assay and that these peptides are able to block drug transport and restore drug sensitivity to MDR cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
peptides can be used to modulate drug transport by P-glycoptein and that this modulation can be used to restore accumulation of chemotherapeutic drugs to the levels found in drug-sensitive cells.

the interaction of hydrophobic peptides with P-gp is not a trivial phenomenon and that it is possible to identify peptides that are able to modulate drug transport by P-gp at concentrations that are not toxic to cells.
the ability of a hydrophobic peptide to interact with the P-glyco protein multidrug transporter can be assessed by a fluorescence-quench assay.
